rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the phrase as a ship loaded to capacity, citing Ubayd ibn al-Abras's use of shahnā as evidence for loading.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: السفينة الموقرة الممتلئة، واستشهد بقول عبيد بن الأبرص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses al-fulk for ships in three named verses and twenty more; falak means an orbit in 21:33 and 36:40, while mashhun accompanies al-fulk only three times.
rows.anchor: وأما مشحون فلم تأت إلا مع الفُلك، في الآيات الثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ship is the immediate sense of al-fulk; the Qur'an's use of safina for Noah's vessel supports it, and safina occurs only in 29:15 and two verses about Moses and his companion.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الفُلْكِ بالسفينة هو القريب المتبادر، ويؤنس إليه أن القرآن استعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding fragment says mayl can mean injustice as deviation from fairness, while ʿawl also conveys constriction and the weight of a burden on its bearer.
rows.anchor: بمعنى الجور ميلا عن الإنصاف. ولا يفوتنا مع هذا التقريب، ما في دلالة العول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses mulim as a sinner or offender, supported by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's poetic use of al-mulim for the wrongdoer.
rows.anchor: قال: وهو مذنب. واستشهد بقول أمية بن أبي الصلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root also appears as malum in singular and plural, as verbs in Yusuf and Ibrahim, as yatalawwamun, as lawmat la'im, and as al-nafs al-lawwama.
rows.anchor: وجاء ملوم، مفرداً في آيات (الذرايات 54، الإسراء 29، 39) وجمعاً

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris defines the root as a sound origin for what takes a person outside the limit of health in any matter.
rows.anchor: قال ابن فارس فى (مرض) : الميم والراء والضاد: أصل صحيح يدل على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qur'anic legal verses, marad, marid, al-marid, and marḍa denote bodily illness; illness of the heart or hearts shifts metaphorically from the root sense.
rows.anchor: فحيثما جاء المرض فى آيات الأحكام فهو من علة فى البدن. وكذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Baqara context explicitly supports reading heart-sickness as hypocrisy; Abu Ubayda glosses it as doubt and hypocrisy, and Maqayis identifies it as hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: وتأويله فى المسألة - فى آية البقرة - بالنفاق، مستفاد من صريح سياقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heart-sickness is broader than hypocrisy: these verses coordinate people with illness in their hearts separately from hypocrites, showing the phrase has a wider sense.
rows.anchor: فشهد بدلالة أعم لمرض فى قلوبهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shatiʾ criticizes traditional accounts of rhetorical inimitability as rigid templates and inflated phrases; even al-Khattabi offered nothing convincing or substantial for modern Arabic readers.
rows.anchor: يدور في هذا النطاق من القوالب التقليدية الصماء والعبارات المضخمة التي لم يجد فيها مثل الخطابي

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر
rows.claim: Abd al-Qahir directs grammatical meanings to their places in the discourse's order, rather than treating parsing as a craft detached from meaning.
rows.anchor: عند عبد القاهر، أن يفهم هذا الإعجاز البلاغي في النظم

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر
rows.claim: His Dalail al-Ijaz presents the knowledge of eloquence as a means to understand the Qur'an's inimitability; a word's excellence depends on how its meaning fits neighboring meanings.
rows.anchor: وكتابه (دلائل الإعجاز) يُفَصَّل القول في هذا العلم الشريف بما يتفاضل به الكلام في نظمه

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر
rows.claim: Words do not differ in merit as isolated forms: fit with adjacent words gives them virtue, and the same word can please in one position yet feel heavy in another.
rows.anchor: فالألفاظ لا تتفاضل من حيث هي ألفاظ مجردة، ولا من حيث هي كلم مفردة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses hamā in the human-creation passages and also in the description of Dhul-Qarnayn's spring as hamia.
rows.anchor: ومعها من كادة حَمَأ، آية الكهف 86

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari reports Qutrub's apparently opposing senses for hamā, but rejects classing them as antonyms because the forms differ and each has only one sense.
rows.anchor: حكاه ابن الأنباري عن قطرب، وقال: وليس هذا عندي من الأضداد

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit defines hamā as black mud and distinguishes removing the mud from putting it into a well; al-Qurtubi cites him on Hijr 15:26.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن السكيت في الأضداد: والحمأ الطين الأسود، وكذلك الحمأة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda reads masnun as poured, from the Arab expression for pouring water; al-Nahhas approves this explanation, as quoted by al-Qurtubi.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة في المجاز: المسنون المصبوب، وهو من قول العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh explains masnun as formed, deriving it from sunnat al-wajh, the face's shape.
rows.anchor: أُخذ من سنة الوجه وهو صورته

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash gives masnun the sense of erected or upright, citing the expression wajh masnun.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفض في المعاني: المسنون المنصوب القائم، من قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same root supplies many forms such as God's sunna and the sunnas of earlier peoples, as well as sinn in the lex talionis phrase 'tooth for tooth.'
rows.anchor: وأما مسنون فجاء من مادتها كثير: سنة الله، وسنتنا، وسنة الأولين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses barikum as your creator and adduces a line by Tubbaʿ as poetic evidence.
rows.anchor: قال: إلى خالقكم. واستشهد بقول تُبَّع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun appears twice in 2:54 and as one of God's beautiful names in 59:24; its verb occurs in 57:22, while the unhamzated bariyya appears in 98:6–7.
rows.anchor: وجاء البارئ اسما من أسماء الله تعالى الحسنى فى آية الحشر 24

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris gives the root two principles: creation and separation or distance from something; barāʾa and tabarruʾ belong to the latter.
rows.anchor: ومادة (برأ) فى مقاييس اللغة أصلان إليهما ترجع فروع الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shatiʾ calls al-Jahiz's Nazm al-Qur'an the only known book arguing that Qur'anic composition is a proof of Muhammad's prophethood, and says its contribution should not be lost.
rows.anchor: ولا يُعرف كتاب فى الاحتجاج لنظم القرآن وعجيب تأليفه وأنه حجة لمحمد على نبوته غير كتاب الجاحظ

rows.speaker: أبو حامد القاضي
rows.claim: Abu Hamid al-Qadi praises Abu Zayd al-Balkhi's book as a uniquely subtle and precise Qur'anic study, despite its author's philosophical views, but says it does not cover every meaning.
rows.anchor: قول أبى حامد القاضى "فى كتاب

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani says Arabic and kalam scholars should have explained the Qur'an's miracle more fully, since the need for this work is urgent and greater than for what they wrote about.
rows.anchor: كما قال القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني في (إعجاز القرآن) :

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani says some scholars' failures led others toward Brahmanist doctrines, taking incomplete and poorly arranged defenses as evidence that the Qur'an has no established miracle.
rows.anchor: وقد قصَّر بعضهم فى هذه المسألة حتى تحول قوم منهم إلى مذاهب البراهمة فيها

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris traces r-k-z to two roots: placing something low within something, as in burying, and sound; rakaz also denotes buried wealth.
rows.anchor: وفي (المقاييس) لمادة ركز أصلان: أحدهما إثبات شيء في شيء يذهب سفلا، والآخر صوت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari transmits Ibn Abbas and others glossing the word as a sound; another group glosses it as a perceptible sense, and Abu Jaafar defines Arab usage as faint sound.
rows.anchor: أسند الطبري عن ابن عباس وغيره، قالوا: صوتا. وعن آخرين: حِساً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound interpretation needs the qualifier faint; Bint al-Shatiʾ finds the alternate gloss 'a sense' closer to the verse's meaning.
rows.anchor: تأويله في المسألة بالصوت، يحتاج إلى قيد بالخفى وأقرب منه: حِساً

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses basira as grim-faced or frowning, citing Ubayd ibn al-Abras's poetic description of a basira troop.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: كالحة، وشاهده قول عبيد بن الأبرص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basira occurs in the faces verse of al-Qiyama, while the related past verb basara appears with ʿabasa in al-Muddaththir.
rows.anchor: ومعها الفعل الماضي في آية المدثر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the phrase as not fearing God's majesty and cites Abu Dhu'ayb's use of yarju for fearing a bee's sting; another wording says not to dread God's majesty.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: لا يخافون لله عظمة. واستشهد بقول أبي ذؤيب

rows.speaker: الأصمعي، أبو حاتم السجستاني، ابن الأنباري، ابن السكيت
rows.claim: The lexicographers list rajaʾ with both senses, hope or desire and fear; Ibn Qutayba classifies rajaw meaning 'feared' among inverted usages and cites Noah 71:13.
rows.anchor: الرجاء في (الأضداد: للأصمعي، وأبي حاتم السجستاني،) وابن الأنباري، وابن السكيت

rows.speaker: السجستاني وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: A dialectal reading understands the phrase as not caring or paying heed; the source associates this usage with Hijaz and several Arab tribes.
rows.anchor: وفي لغة كنانة وخزاعة ونصر وهذيل، بمعنى المبالاة

rows.speaker: الجمهرة من أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Most exegetes take it to mean that Noah's people do not fear or heed God's majesty.
rows.anchor: والجمهرة من أهل التأويل على أن معناها في آية نوح: لا تخافون لله عظمة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari instead reads rajaʾ as hope: why do they not hope for God's honoring them in the abode of reward? He links waqar to the addressees and cites the fronted lillah.
rows.anchor: سوى الزمخشري فإنه ذهب إلى أنها بمعنى الأمل. وعلق الوقار بالمخاطبين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra rejects the grammarians' claim that la is merely extra: the Qur'anic denial responds to those who denied resurrection, paradise, and hell, as la wallahi can answer prior speech.
rows.anchor: قال "الفراء" يرد على قول كثير من النحويين بأنها صلة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: For al-Farra, deleting la would erase the difference between an oath answering earlier speech and a newly initiated oath, so the particle has a meaningful responsive role.
rows.anchor: ولو ألقيت "لا" مما يُنوَى به الجواب، لم يكن بين اليمين التي تكون جواباً

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham summarizes views that la is emphatic extra, or negates an earlier claim in another sura before a new oath; the Qur'an can work as one sura, with answers across suras.
rows.anchor: في القرن الثامن، جاء بها "ابن هشام" في باب "لا، الزائدة في الكلام لمجرد تقويته وتأكيده"

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses banan as the fingertips and cites Antara's line about warriors holding reins by their fingers.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: أطراف الأصابع. وشاهده قول عنترة العبسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banan is the plural or collective form related to banana and denotes fingers or their tips; the lexicon notes it can mean a single finger.
rows.anchor: البَنان واحدته بنانة، وهى الأصابع أو أطرافها

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports three readings of banan in the battle verse: tips of fingers and toes, extremities generally, or every joint.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هى الأطراف، وقيل: كل مفصل (الطبرى)

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan records those alternatives but prefers the reading that banan means fingers.
rows.anchor: حكاها أبوحيان وقال: والمختار أنها الأصابع

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib also interprets banan as fingers, specified because people use them to fight and defend themselves.
rows.anchor: وفسرها الراغب كذلك بالأصابع، خصها الله تعالى بالذكر لأجل أنهم بها يقاتلون ويدافعون

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله بن عمرو الأنصاري
rows.claim: Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Amr al-Ansari said he recognized his father, martyred at Uhud, only by his fingertips.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث جابر، بن عبد الله بن عمرو الأنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses banan only in the al-Anfal battle verse and the resurrection passage in al-Qiyama.
rows.anchor: وليس القرآن غيرهما من المادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadaiq occurs in al-Naba 78:32, Abasa 80:30, and al-Naml 27:60; no other Qur'anic words come from this root.
rows.anchor: وليس في القرآن من المادة، غير هذه الكلمات الثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Translating hadaiq simply as bustan imports a Persian loanword and misses the Arabic sense; the Qur'an does not use bustan.
rows.anchor: واضح أن تفسير الحدائق بالبساتين، هو من التفسير بمعرَّبٍ من لغة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic a hadiqah is what is enclosed by a structure of trees or palms; usage later extended to a palm grove because it surrounds the area.
rows.anchor: والعربية تستعمل الحديقة، فيما يحدق به بناء، من شجر أو نخل

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib derives hadiqah by analogy with the eye's garden, based on its shape and the gathering of water within it.
rows.anchor: وذهب "الراغب" في المفردات، إلى أنها سميت حديقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Ibn al-Azraq question-and-answer entry, muqitan is glossed as capable, with Ahiyaha ibn al-Jalah cited as evidence that Arabs used the word this way.
rows.anchor: قال: قادرا. قال: وهل كانت العرب تعرف ذلك؟ قال: نعم

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani's al-Risala al-Shafiya develops his argument for Qur'anic inimitability; he considers it persuasive to someone with receptive taste, but not to one lacking the faculty to understand it.
rows.anchor: ومع الدلائل، قدم الجرجاني (الرسالة الشافية) فى إعجاز القرآن

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani compares understanding this rhetorical field to judging poetry: without the requisite taste, someone may wrongly assume they possess the needed competence and issue uninformed judgments.
rows.anchor: وكما لا يقيم الشعر فى نفس من لا ذوق له، لا يفهم هذا البابَ

rows.speaker: عبد القاهر الجرجاني
rows.claim: He says argument works only with a listener willing to attend and follow its direction; then resistance can turn into ease and acceptance.
rows.anchor: حتى تجد مَن فيه عون لك، ومن إذا أبى عليك أي ذاك طبعُه فردَّه إليك

rows.speaker: ابن حزم الظاهري
rows.claim: Bint al-Shatiʾ notes that Ibn Hazm, in the fifth century, challenged earlier writers on inimitability and sharply criticized al-Baqillani.
rows.anchor: فى القرن الخامس أيضاً، ظهر ابن حزم الظاهرى (ت 456 هـ) فتصدى للسلف ممن تكلموا فى إعجاز القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A transmission glosses naqir as what appears on a date stone where the palm sprouts and cites a poet's line as evidence.
rows.anchor: ما ظهر النواة ومنه تنبت النخلة. وشاهده في الثلاثة قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naqir occurs in the two cited verses in al-Nisa; the same root also appears in the trumpet phrase in al-Muddaththir.
rows.anchor: ومن المادة: {فَإِذَا نُقِرَ فِي النَّاقُورِ} بآية المدثر 8

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Farra provide a clearer gloss: the small indentation on the back of a date stone.
rows.anchor: أوضح منه قول أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like fatil and qitmir, naqir is a figurative kenning for something tiny, insignificant, and worthless, rather than its literal physical feature.
rows.anchor: غير مراد بها أصل معناها، بل المراد المعنى المجازي كناية عن الضئيل الحقير

rows.speaker: الأساس
rows.claim: Al-Asas gives the literal origin as the small mark on the back of the date stone.
rows.anchor: وأصل النقير النكتة التي في ظهر النواة
